#2708. Cardinals reportedly fear QB Gardner Minshew has torn UCL, could miss remainder of season

The Arizona Cardinals are awaiting additional tests on quarterback Gardner Minshew's elbow.

According to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, the concern is that the QB has torn the UCL in his throwing elbow and would miss the rest of the season, with months of rehab ahead.

If Minshew is out for the rest of the season, rookie quarterback Carson Beck, the Cardinals' third-round draft pick this year, would be in line to start.

On the final play of the first half of the Seahawks' 17-3 win, Donte Fowler hit Minshew coming around the offensive line. The quarterback was in the middle of throwing, and his arm bent at an odd angle as he forced the pass.

Beck started warming up, but Minshew didn't miss any snaps in the game.

The loss against Seattle was Minshew's first start of the season, after he replaced Jacoby Brissett in the team's comeback overtime win over the Dallas Cowboys. Minshew has thrown for 354 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions in two games this year.

Minshew's promotion to starter also came after Brissett was traded to the Baltimore Ravens last week.

With Beck as the only other quarterback in Arizona's organization, the team is reportedly signing career backup Josh Johnson off the Cleveland Browns' practice squad, per ESPN's Adam Schefter. The Cardinals will be Johnson's 15th NFL team in his 14-year career.

Beck has not yet played in a regular season game. The rookie played extensively in Arizona's first preseason action against the Carolina Panthers in the Hall of Fame Game.

The quarterback completed 15 of 19 passes for 188 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions, in the loss to the Panthers. Beck suffered a rib injury during the game that sidelined him for the rest of the preseason.

Minshew isn't the only potential season-ending injury that Arizona is dealing with. Wide receiver Michael Wilson fractured something in his neck, according to head coach Mike LaFleur, and will miss the remainder of the season.

The Cardinals play the Los Angeles Rams this week. Arizona then has the Kansas City Chiefs, Washington Commanders and Philadelphia Eagles, then a Week 14 bye.

Arizona is 3-6 and last in the NFC West. With the trade decisions made earlier in the year and the high-profile injuries suffered last week, the rest of the season may be an evaluation of the team's young talent.

#2707. Kevin McGonigle, Sal Stewart win BBWAA Rookie of the Year Awards

Awards Season is officially in full swing now, as the BBWAA will be announcing the winners of their annual awards throughout the week. As usual, the ceremonies got started off with the BBWAA Jackie Robinson Rookie of the Year Awards and the flavor of this year's edition was Central Divison-centric.

Indeed, Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Sal Stewart of the Cincinnati Reds ended up taking home the hardware for the AL And NL Rookie of the Year Awards, respectively.

When it comes to the AL race, it was really no contest as McGonigle finished with 28 of the possible 30 first place votes on his way to becoming the sixth Rookie of the Year Award for Detroit winner — their first winner since 2016 which is when Michael Fullmer took home the honors. McGonigle finished the year with a slash line of .278/.376/.430 with a .357 wOBA, 129 wRC+ and 18 home runs while splitting time equally between shortstop and third base. McGonigle finished the season as the rookie leader in fWAR at 5.4, so it's not particularly shocking that he took home the honors.

The NL Race wasn't much closer, as Sal Stewart ended up taking home the honors in comfortable fashion as he received 20 of the 30 possible first place votes. Stewart's award now makes it nine times that Reds players have won this award now, with the most recent winner before Sal being Jonathan India back in 2021. Stewart finished his year with a .263/.330/.457 line along with a .339 wOBA, 112 wRC+ and 32 dingers on the year. Stewart led all NL rookies in homers, but I will say that it's kind of shocking that JJ Wetherholt not only didn't win it but he also finished third behind Carson Benge as well.

With all of that being said, our very own Didier Fuentes did receive some consideration for this award. Atlanta's top reliever (according to Walt Weiss, himself) earned two fifth-place votes in order to come in eighth-place overall in the NL Rookie of the Year voting, so it's at least nice to see that Fuentes's efforts on the mound this season (58 appearances, 73.1 innings pitched, 2.45 ERA (58 ERA-), 2.60 FIP (62 FIP-) didn't go completely ignored.

BBWAA Awards Week will continue tomorrow night, as we'll find out if Walt Weiss did enough to earn the honors of being NL Manager of the Year. We'll see what happens then.

#2706. Effenberg responds to Hoeneß's Musiala comments amid Bayern contract concerns

Speaking on SPORT1’s Doppelpass programme, Effenberg suggested Bayern could be reconsidering the financial commitment made to Musiala, given the limited return they have received amid his fitness struggles.

“On the one hand, there’s the illness, and on the other, his injury history. They may be wondering whether it was too much given what they are currently getting in return, or considering the difficult situation they now find themselves in,” Effenberg explained.

The 23-year-old Germany international signed a long-term contract extension with Bayern in February 2025, committing his future to the club until 2030. However, his subsequent injury struggles have limited his availability, with the midfielder having endured a particularly difficult period following a serious ankle injury sustained at the Club World Cup in July 2025.

Effenberg believes there is a clear distinction between Musiala’s situation and that of Harry Kane, whose recent contract extension he considers an entirely straightforward decision for the Bayern hierarchy.

“Everyone would agree that Harry Kane’s new contract was the right decision and entirely understandable. I believe the Bayern hierarchy are more concerned about Jamal Musiala’s contract,” the former midfielder added.

Despite questioning whether Bayern may have second thoughts about the terms of Musiala’s deal, Effenberg was keen to stress that neither the player nor the club should be held responsible for the circumstances.

“Nobody is to blame for the situation, neither the player nor the club,” he concluded.

Musiala remains an important part of Bayern’s long-term plans, but his availability will inevitably be a significant consideration as the German champions look to get the best possible return from their investment in one of the country’s most talented attacking midfielders.

#2702. Moments that mattered: Ohio State fends off Marshall, 84-74

The Ohio State men's basketball team returned to their home court on Monday night, three days after dispatching in-state foe Youngstown State, 89-65, for their first win of the new season. The Buckeyes' tangoed with Marshall for the third time ever, with the last game against the Thundering Herd coming back on November 25, 2016. That game was during Thad Matta's final season at the helm of the program, and Ohio State won that game, 111-70.

The Buckeyes stuck with the same starting lineup they used in the first two games of the season — fan favorites John Mobley Jr. and Amare Bynum were flanked by three new faces — Anthony Thompson, Justin Pippen, and Andrija Jelavic.

Unlike Friday night, it took Ohio State less than seven minutes to open up a double-digit lead on the visiting team on Monday. After Marshall's Luke Rasmussen split a pair of free throws to get the Herd back within 10-9, Ohio State went on a 12-0 run over the next 3:07 to open things up and take a 22-9 lead. By the time the second media timeout rolled around with 10:47 left in the half, the Buckeyes had a 25-11 lead.

During that run, Jimmie Williams came off the bench and knocked down his first three-pointer of the season, and also slithered into the paint through several Marshall defenders to drop in a very difficult layup off the right side of the glass. Thompson also hit his first three-pointer of his college career during that massive Ohio State run in the first half.

With Thompson and Williams lighting it up, the Buckeyes tried to push their lead to 20 points by halftime, but didn't quite get there. Ohio State took a 45-27 lead into the locker room at halftime, and shot 43.8% as a team. They likely would've been ahead by a whole lot more if it wasn't for Marshall's Noah Otshudi, who was doing major work for the Thundering Herd on the other side. The senior guard from Ontario, Canada scored 22 points in Marshall's last game (a loss to Toledo), and followed it up by scoring 15 points on 7-for-12 shooting in the first half alone on Monday. Unfortunately for Otshudi, the rest of his team combined to shoot 29.4% (5-for-12) in the first half.

Otshudi kept torching Ohio State to start the second half, scoring three times in the first 91 seconds of the second half to help Marshall cut the Buckeyes' lead to 48-36. Diebler called a timeout, but it didn't change much as the Thundering Herd came out of that timeout and scored seven straight to cut the lead to 48-43, forcing Diebler to call his second timeout in less than three minutes. The duo of Otshudi and Bryce Slay were causing problems for Ohio State, and the Buckeyes were not taking care of the ball on the other end as their lead withered away at a rapid pace.

Once the lead was cut to five, Bynum dug in and scored on back-to-back possessions for Ohio State, giving the Buckeyes a double-digit lead once again. Last year, you'd likely see Bruce Thornton as the go-to option when the game appeared to reach a breaking point. On Monday night, it was Bynum who came up with two big baskets when the Buckeyes had their backs against the wall. Williams then followed up Bynum's five points with a floater, turning it into a 7-0 run that put the Buckeyes ahead 55-43 with 14:30 remaining.

Marshall kept hanging around, and two free throws from Fazl Oshodi cut the lead back to six points, 68-62, with 6:43 left in the game. The teams went almost two minutes without anyone scoring until Curtis Givens knocked down a corner three to put Ohio State up 71-62,

The Thundering Herd never went away, fighting Ohio State until the very bitter end, with Jelavic's pair of free throws giving Ohio State a double-digit lead once again, 81-70, with one minute left in the game. That was the final dagger for the Thundering Herd, as Ohio State escaped with an 84-74 win.

Ohio State does not return home again for a week — they welcome the Prairie View A&M Panthers next Monday at 6:30 p.m. at the Schottenstein Center. Between now and then, the Buckeyes will travel to Hartford, Connecticut to tangle with the No. 4 UConn Huskies. That game is the front of a two-year home-and-home series, with the Huskies coming to Columbus next season.

The Buckeyes picked up their second win of the season Monday evening, making Ohio State a perfect 3-0 against Marshall all-time. Here are a few of the moments that mattered from the 84-74 victory:

You could argue that Ohio State had gotten essentially zero production out of two of the top six guys in their playing rotation through two games, with Thompson and Williams combining for 14 points on 2-for-21 shooting while going a perfect 10-for-10 at the free throw line.

Thompson and Williams both knocked down their first three-pointers of the season in the first half of Monday nights game, with Williams finally seeing one go through at the 14:38 mark to give Ohio State a 13-9 lead, and Thompson connecting from deep three minutes later to make it 25-11 Buckeyes.

Thompson and Williams were Ohio State's leading scorers in the first half, with Williams scoring 12 points on 4-for-7 shooting and Thompson chipping in 10 on 3-for-6 shooting.

Marshall's struggles in the first half could not be blamed on the Thundering Herd's senior guard and returning leading scorer from last season. The 6-foot-4 guard from Ontario had 15 of Marshall's 27 points in the first half, while the rest of the Thundering Herd combined for 12 points on 5-for-12 shooting.

Otshudi came into Monday's game averaging 19 points per game, and surpassed that less than two minutes into the second half. He scored Marshall's first six points of second half to get him to 21 points with 18:29 left in the game.

After the Thundering Herd stampeded out of the locker room and opened the second half on a 16-3 run to cut the lead from 18 to five points, someone had to take a stand for Ohio State, and on Monday it was sophomore forward Amare Bynum.

With Ohio State clinging to a 48-43 lead with 15:07 left in the game, Bynum backed down his defender and scored below the basket, pushing the lead back to seven points. After Marshall's Vasilije Kuridza was called for an offensive foul, Mobley brought the ball down and dumped the ball off to Bynum, who scored while being fouled. Bynum hit the free throw to complete the three-point play, capping off a mini 5-0 run by himself and putting Ohio State ahead by 10 again, 53-43, with 14:47 left in the game.

After a Manyuon jumper cut the lead to 58-49, Josh Ojianwuna was fouled going to the basket. He hit both free throws, putting Ohio State ahead 60-49 with 12:09 let in the game. On the very next Marshall possession, he cleanly picked Manyuon's pocket, and Thompson was able to jump on the ball before he was fouled by Manyuon. It went down in the box score as a steal for Thompson, but Ojianwuna very much created the havoc that led to the steal.

With the Buckeyes up 79-70 and 1:04 left on the clock, Mobley tried to knock down a three-point dagger to ice the game. He missed, but Jelavic was there to clean up the mess, and was fouled by Marshall's Luke Rasmussen. Jelavic hit both free throws to give Ohio State an 81-70 lead — the first time they'd been up double digits in almost three minutes.

#2700. Mike McCarthy: Steelers improved since last Bengals matchup

The Steelers and Bengals will meet for the second time this season on Sunday — a game between two 6-2 teams that will end with one moving into sole possession of first place in the AFC North.

The last time Pittsburgh played the Bengals, the Steelers won 30-27 at home on Sept. 27. And talking to the media on Monday, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said he'd "like the outcome to be the same" when the two teams clash again in Week 10.

However, McCarthy acknowledged things will be different this week. This time, the game will be in Cincinnati, and on Sunday Night Football instead of the 1 p.m. EST time slot. Pittsburgh will be without Roman Wilson and could still be missing Michael Pittman Jr. at the wide receiver poison.

But Pittsburgh has also improved in the weeks between the Bengals matchups, the Steelers head coach said.

"I think we're playing differently than we were the first time around," McCarthy said. "I think we're better … I think we're definitely performing better in the trenches. I think, offensively, our ball distribution is better."

The Week 3 Bengals game was Pittsburgh's first with Brock Hoffman and Max Iheanachor on the starting offensive line. It was also Jaylen Warren's first 100-yard game of the season.

McCarthy also credited with the defense with taking "a big step."

"I think the pressure, particularly in the last game, is something that will serve us very well moving forward against anybody," he said. The Steelers managed eight sacks against the Browns in their last game in Week 8.

"I think teams change," McCarthy said. "It's not who you're playing — it's when you play them. It's November football. I think our football team is starting to reflect that. I think that's what's most important."

McCarthy said he watched the Bengals' Week 9 game, a 34-17 drubbing of the Falcons in Madrid, live over the Steelers' bye week. He said Cincinnati "looked great" on offense, but pushed back on talking about how the Bengals have changed since Week 3.

"I wouldn't say 'change,'" McCarthy said. "I think Joe (Burrow) is on top of his game. That was an impressive oﬀensive performance yesterday. They're rolling. … I think that's the whole thing, is just make sure we're dialed in on how we want to play and in touch with the matchups, ball distribution. I think (Burrow's) time clock — the way he distributes the football and the connection he has with his receivers — is top notch."

Burrow currently ranks second in the NFL in passing yards with 2,386. His 23 passing touchdowns are the most in the league. Cincinnati also has two receivers in the top 15 for receiving yardage in Tee Higgins (758, six touchdowns) and Ja'Marr Chase (647, seven touchdowns).

McCarthy said it was "fair" to say that the Steelers have a better handle on their secondary since the last Bengals game, when Joey Porter Jr. was still on the roster although not playing.

"We've played eight games now," he said. "We've had a chance to go through game plans. We've had a chance to build game plans as a staﬀ and with our players. We've had game day sideline adjustments. So, I think you could really say that for the whole team, as far as where we are today compared to where we were when we played them the first time."

McCarthy stressed the importance of combating Burrow's ability to stay on time in the pocket and negate a pass rush; the Steelers only logged one sack in Week 3.

"I think we're in a rotation now. We're in a good rhythm," McCarthy said of the Steelers' pass rush, now tied for third in the NFL with 26 sacks. "I think that's all part of it. … I love the way our veteran guys communicate with our coaches and the younger guys. I think Cam (Heyward) and T.J. (Watt), and just the level of communication, the things they see and the adjustments they're making for pass rush and creating those opportunities. So, that's where things become a half second quicker."

Even if the pressure doesn't result in a sack, McCarthy said "the little things matter."

"The pressure, that's the diﬀerence between hitting the arm of the quarterback or bull rushing the A-gap where the quarterback can't step into the throw," he said. "I just think we're better today than we were back four or five weeks ago."

Backup quarterback Shedeur Sanders started and nearly pulled off an overtime comeback win, but fell just short on a failed two-point conversion as the Saints won 23-22.

With the wideout in concussion protocol, his status for the Bears' next game is uncertain. Burden, however, will be helped by the Bears being on a bye in Week 10, giving him an additional week to recover from the injury before Chicago takes the field again.

#2694. Fantasy Football Booms and Busts: Mega-star WRs show out in otherwise wonky Week 9

In the middle of a wonky Week 9, I looked to the wide receiver board for comfort. Maybe some alpha wideouts posting big numbers would soothe the nerves a little bit. Alas, even that roundup brought some agita. The NFL is a whirlwind, now and forever.

The Week 9 receivers on the outside are names you know by heart. CeeDee Lamb (10-195-1) went bananas with George Pickens unavailable. Puka Nacua (14-150-1) was unstoppable against Washington, the one reliable downfield option Matthew Stafford has. Ja'Marr Chase (10-155-1) was worth the early alarm, torching the Falcons in Spain. And in the later window, the newly Green Bay stars, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, crushed against the New England secondary.

But the breaking Nacua news overshadows the day. Nacua was hurt on his final snap against the Commanders — on an endgame running play of all things — and needs an MRI on his knee Monday. The Rams don't believe Nacua has a torn ACL, but any MRI is a scary prospect. Nacua's production over the last six games has been too good to be true: 84 targets, 65 catches, 641 yards, five total touchdowns.

The funny thing about the Rams, even with Nacua going nuclear, the L.A. offense hasn't been special. It's scored a modest 44 points in the last two weeks, despite playing the Chargers and Commanders. There was the 18-16 loss to Arizona in Week 6. Forget the Rams as preseason favorites; they're no guarantee to be a playoff team. And if Nacua misses time, all bets are clearly off.

Lamb is doing the target thing for the Cowboys, too. He had 16 looks in the win at Indianapolis, what we want from our first-rounders. That makes 83 targets in six games for Lamb, and while the Pickens' absence made it easier for Prescott to look Lamb's way, the Cowboys will always lean that way. San Francisco is a challenge next week, then come favorable draws against Tennessee and Philadelphia.

I was hopeful Ryan Flournoy would spread his wings without Pickens, but that narrative died on the vine. Flournoy had a late 46-yard catch to partially save his day, but a 2-53-0 log on three targets goes down as a loss. It just underscores the variance at the receiver position — Flournoy had four productive weeks as the team's No. 3 receiver, then was mostly invisible here.

Joe Burrow and the Bengals are usually a palate-cleaning offense, and Week 9 applies. The Bengals romped over Atlanta 34-17 in the morning game, with Burrow throwing for three scores and running in another. Burrow steered most of the work to Chase (12 targets), though Tee Higgins salvaged a 5-32-2 day on his six opportunities. Ah, touchdown deodorant.

But not everything is sunshine and lollipops in Cincinnati. Chase Brown continues to be a net loss for fantasy managers, getting just 12 chances and making a credible 75 yards. The efficiency is good, the workload was not. He also didn't score a touchdown; he's stuck on one for the year. Samaje Perine (11-43-0) is playing more than anyone imagined, and with the Bengals legitimate AFC contenders again, you wonder if the team would explore the RB market over the next two days.

— The Texans continue to play against type, a pass-first offense with a stagnant running game and a defense that's far less than expected. C.J. Stroud continued his redemption song, throwing for five touchdowns and 384 yards against the sorry Chargers. The Houston passing tree continues to be wide, as Kayshon Boutte (4-125-2) and Tank Dell (4-105-1) had the most productive days, and Nico Collins was targeted just four times (4-55-1). Before the year, we thought this would be a small pie with Collins getting the biggest piece; it's turned into a larger pie, but the shares are split rather evenly. The Browns are next up.

— Familiar names pushed back to the top of the running back board, with Kenneth Walker III, Bijan Robinson and Christian McCaffrey all scoring well. Walker had three total touchdowns, two in the receiving game, and the Falcons finally got Robinson going again in their passing game (47 yards). McCaffrey continues to be ordinary in efficiency, but a couple of scores got him home in a lopsided win over the Raiders. Widely available Jordan Watkins (4-86-1) was the best of the San Francisco receivers, scoring on a nifty, contested catch in the end zone.

— I was hopeful that Alvin Kamara could get a bigger role with Kendre Miller cut, but the Saints dialed up Audric Estime (15-72-1) as the primary back against the Browns. Maybe it's not a surprise that Estime was used, but I didn't expect him to be this effective. Chris Olave (7-98-0) was the target hog for the Saints, though rookie Jordyn Tyson (4-30-0) had five targets and lost a touchdown at the one-yard line. The Saints still haven't scored a first-quarter touchdown all year, but Tyler Shough usually has credible fantasy stats when the day is over.

— Detroit games are usually a blast on both sides of the ball, but just 498 yards of offense hit the field between the Lions and Dolphins. Jared Goff was limited to 170 yards and no touchdowns — although the Miami defense isn't great, it's not a punching bag, either. Jahmyr Gibbs had a 20-74-1 rushing log but no receptions. Malik Willis was one of my favorite Week 9 sleepers, but this one stayed asleep — no touchdowns, just 135 total yards. Perhaps the groin injury he dealt with this week was more of a problem on Sunday than anticipated.

— Usually, solving for volume will get you fantasy glory, but Devin Singletary did very little with 23 touches (just 39 total yards). The lone New York touchdown was a Jameis Winston pass to Isaiah Likely — Winston briefly replaced an injured J.J. McCarthy. McCarthy didn't have his best showing, posting a 6.7 YPA and taking five sacks. The Eagles offense stayed shipwrecked, though a 22-yard Saquon Barkley day was at least helped by a short touchdown run. There are too many dead offenses in fantasy; the Eagles are perilously close to becoming one. Barkley was always a back-nine player, but maybe he's teeing off on the 18th.

— The Jets at times have been a fun fantasy offense, but it's not always easy to read the pregame signals. Last week it was Omar Cooper Jr. toasting a bagel while Adonai Mitchell went off — at Kansas City, Cooper spread his wings (8-58-0) in a PPR scam, but Mitchell went catchless on seven targets (a bushel of air yards, and at least two drops). We expected better with Garrett Wilson out. Breece Hall and Braelon Allen both made 4.1 YPC with their work, though Hall had 15 rushes to Allen's eight. The Jets perhaps were showcasing Hall, someone who should draw interest as we close in on Tuesday's trading deadline.

— Jonah Coleman didn't look special at Carolina, but 21 touches, 88 yards and a score validated anyone who started him. Meanwhile, J.K. Dobbins was limited to just five touches. Pat Bryant returned and scored a touchdown, but it's still so hard to recommend anyone in this passing game. Courtland Sutton also had a TD, but 5-45-1 is a modest return on nine targets. Nobody really believes in the Broncos, even with that 7-2 record.

— Given that he was up against the Denver defense, Bryce Young took a step in the right direction (three touchdowns, one pick, 7.1 YPA, 106.4 rating). But it was surprising to see veteran TE Darren Waller operating as the target hog (10 looks, 8-90-1), not Tetairoa McMillen (4-56-1) or Jalen Coker (4-29-0). Chuba Hubbard didn't score but grinded out 96 yards on 20 touches. He brings a nice floor every week, as no one is pushing him in this backfield.

— Seattle always wants to have a backfield platoon and that's what went down against Arizona. Zach Charbonnet was the runner (16-77-0, 17 touches), Jadarian Price the receiver (4-54-0, 13 touches). But just to kick everyone in the shins, tight end AJ Barner stole a short touchdown on a goal-line push. Barner was highly effective in short yardage last year, so this could have some stickiness moving forward.

— Does anyone ever really win with the Las Vegas backfield? Certainly not in Week 9. Mike Washington went for minus-3 yards on six carries, and somehow Ashton Jeanty had minus-5 yards on five short receptions. Not exactly Thunder and Lightning here. The schedule gets worse, with Seattle and Denver up next. Jeanty and Washington are desperation plays at best right now.

#2692. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2689. AL Rookie of the Year: Why I voted for the Guardians' Parker Messick over the Tigers' Kevin McGonigle

Parker Messick is now in a club all by himself.

On Wednesday, the Cleveland Guardians' left-hander will likely finish third in AL Cy Young voting behind Yankees ace Cam Schlittler and Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease. Messick being announced as a finalist confirmed him as just the sixth rookie in MLB history to finish in the top three of Cy Young voting, joining Mark Fidrych (1976), Fernando Valenzuela (1981), Dwight Gooden (1984), Jose Fernandez (2013) and Paul Skenes (2024).

All five previous rookie Cy Young finalists were named Rookie of the Year for their standout debut campaigns. But on Monday, Messick finished second in 2026 AL Rookie of the Year voting behind Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle, who received 28 out of 30 first-place votes.

This outcome says plenty about just how special of a season McGonigle put together on his way to surpassing Messick in this race. And as one of the two voters who put Messick first on their ballot, I can now discuss how I arrived at that conclusion.

This was not an easy decision, and it became only more difficult as neither Messick nor McGonigle faltered down the stretch of the regular season. To be clear, McGonigle is quite obviously a worthy winner. Watching the early stages of his career has been an absolute treat, as he quickly proved that his special hit tool, lauded by scouts during his high school days, translates seamlessly to the pro ranks.

Since he was drafted in 2023, I watched from afar as McGonigle tore through the minor leagues. Then I got my first in-person look last year in the Arizona Fall League, where he was the best player in the league by a mile and also one of the youngest. His brilliant 2025 across three levels of the minors launched him into the highest rung of top prospect lists, alongside Pittsburgh's Konnor Griffin and Milwaukee's Jesus Made. And of those three, it was McGonigle who made the big-league team out of spring training and wasted no time announcing his presence, with four hits in his major-league debut on Opening Day.

After four games batting sixth, McGonigle never hit lower than third in Detroit's lineup for the remainder of the season. Meanwhile, the 21-year-old bounced between shortstop and third base, depending on what the Tigers needed. I watched him in person on multiple occasions in 2026, including at the All-Star Game in Philadelphia, where he was the youngest player on either roster. A few weeks later, I was in Detroit when he walked off the Dodgers during Tarik Skubal's emotional homecoming weekend, offering a resounding reminder that the Tigers' future is still bright with McGonigle leading the way.

There's no shortage of stats indicating that McGonigle's season was special, but by the end, it was the consistency and bulk of excellence that stood out. From Opening Day through September, McGonigle was a dependable, daily fixture in Detroit's lineup en route to an AL-leading 707 plate appearances — the most by a rookie since Ichiro Suzuki (738) and Jimmy Rollins (720) in 2001.

It's no surprise, then, that the Tigers felt comfortable making an enormous commitment to McGonigle, inking an eight-year, $150 million extension just a few weeks into his career. He's that good. And if you're asking me whom I'd rather have on my team moving forward, I'd take McGonigle over not only Messick but also almost any other young position player in the game today. But in trying to assess which rookie season was more impressive, I ended up leaning toward Messick, if ever so slightly.

WAR (Wins Above Replacement) is an easy place to start when sorting through any modern award race, but it didn't really do me any favors here. While WAR is an outstanding, catch-all measure of all-around value, I'm less inclined to rely on it when two players are within 1 WAR of each other. That was the case with McGonigle and Messick by all three of the most prominent metrics: Baseball Reference (bWAR) had McGonigle at 7.1 to Messick's 6.3, FanGraphs (fWAR) had McGonigle at 5.4 to Messick's 4.9, and Baseball Prospectus (WARP) had McGonigle at 5.2 to Messick's 4.9.

McGonigle's 7.1 bWAR led all AL players (hitters and pitchers) in 2026. It was the seventh-most by a rookie position player since integration (1947) and the most by a rookie since Aaron Judge's 8.1 in 2017. Messick's 6.3 bWAR was third in the AL behind McGonigle and presumptive AL Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler (7.0). His mark rated similarly historically among rookies, tied for seventh among rookie pitchers since integration and the most by a rookie pitcher since Mark Eichhorn's 7.3 in 1986. By fWAR, Messick stands out even more historically. His 4.9 is tied with six others (including Valenzuela and Spencer Strider) for eighth among rookie pitchers since integration, while McGonigle's 5.4 is tied with recent rookie standouts Jackson Merrill and Corbin Carroll for 21st among position players.

With WAR failing to give me a decisive answer, I dug into the degree to which each candidate stood out relative to not only their first-year peers but also the league as a whole. It was apparent by midsummer that McGonigle and Messick had separated themselves from the rest of the rookie pack. So how did their performances stack up against the big leagues' best hitters and pitchers, regardless of experience? This framing, in a nutshell, is what tilted me toward Messick.

Messick was not a premier prospect like McGonigle, but he wasn't a total nobody, either. Unheralded at a Tampa-area high school, the lefty blossomed into a brilliant college pitcher at Florida State. Still, his modest stature and lack of impact velocity limited his prospect stock leading up to the 2022 draft, in which the Guardians took him in the second round. He climbed Cleveland's minor-league system methodically, flummoxing opposing hitters with his funky uptempo delivery and pinpoint command. He made his major-league debut on Aug. 20, 2025, and quietly shined down the stretch, posting a 2.72 ERA across 39 ⅔ innings.

Messick's stellar first impression boosted his status in scouting circles — you could find him in the bottom 20 of most top-100 prospect lists entering 2026. Still, he did not arrive at spring camp with a guaranteed rotation spot. In fact, it was not until the final days of spring training that he secured a role on Cleveland's starting staff, making him the Guardians' No. 5 starter to begin the year. But it didn't take long for him to shed that label and emerge as a legitimate frontline arm.

In 2026, Messick was one of just 22 hurlers league-wide to make at least 32 regular-season starts. And not only did he log more innings (186 ⅓) than any rookie since Sandy Alcantara in 2019 (197 ⅓) but he also did it in an era in which such workloads are rarer than ever. This year, Messick was one of just 13 pitchers to clear the 180-inning threshold; that's by far the fewest 180-inning pitchers MLB has ever produced in a non-shortened season, breaking the previous record of 20 in 2021. A decade ago, that number was 46. In 2006, it was 70.

And Messick wasn't just eating innings. Among 46 qualified starters, he ranked sixth in ERA (2.56), ninth in FIP (3.07), eighth in WHIP (1.063) and ninth in OPS allowed (.623). His four-seam fastball — which spiked from sitting 92 mph as a prospect to averaging 94.4 mph and climbing as high as 98 mph — ranked as the fifth-most valuable individual pitch in the majors by run value and accounted for 101 of his 193 strikeouts. Another 71 of those punchouts came courtesy of Messick's terrific changeup; only Cristopher Sánchez produced more strikeouts via cambio in 2026.

Across the 2026 season, the reliability of Messick's run prevention was staggering. His ERA over such a sizable sample of innings was remarkable; among 115 qualified rookie pitchers in the wild-card era (since 1995), only Fernandez in 2013 (2.19) and Hideo Nomo in 1995 (2.54) logged lower ERAs. This was possible because of Messick's ability to avoid the kind of total clunkers that would single-handedly damage his sterling stats. He never allowed more than four earned runs in an outing, and even that happened only three times. Messick delivered 18 starts with one or zero earned runs allowed, third-most in the majors behind only Cy Young favorites Schlittler (25) and Jacob Misiorowski (20). He completed five innings in all but two starts — and one of those was an abbreviated outing in Game 162 as Cleveland prepared for the postseason.

Speaking of the postseason: It does seem that Messick's outlier workload caught up to him in October, when his command uncharacteristically faltered across four postseason starts, three of which Cleveland lost. While he was far from the only one responsible for Cleveland's postseason exit, Messick's relatively lackluster showing as one of the team's best players was disappointing in the context of Cleveland's push to end MLB's longest World Series drought.

That said, the Guardians wouldn't have even sniffed a first-round bye without Messick's contributions in the regular season. And with my ROY ballot due before postseason games began, I felt comfortable putting Messick atop my ballot, based on what had transpired over the previous six months.

Across the 2026 season, McGonigle managed to live up to the sky-high expectations — that's no small feat — and he is most certainly deserving of Rookie of the Year honors. But Messick delivered beyond the preseason projections and then some, putting together a historic rookie campaign of his own. In the end, I decided he did enough to earn my vote.

3. Chase DeLauter, Guardians4. Payton Tolle, Red Sox5. Munetaka Murakami, White Sox

For third place, it was a coin-toss between Tolle and DeLauter, both of whom wowed me throughout their rookie campaigns. I ended up going with DeLauter due to his season-long steadiness as Cleveland's best bat. Talent has never been a question for the 25-year-old, but a litany of injuries have limited his availability since he was selected in the first round in 2022. But this season, DeLauter and the Guardians collaborated on a plan to effectively manage his workload, and he amassed 559 plate appearances across 133 games played, including 69 starts in right field and 60 at DH.

And when available, DeLauter delivered excellent results: His 131 wRC+ was not just tops among AL rookies (ahead of even McGonigle) but also 10th among qualified AL hitters. He was one of just four AL sluggers to post a slugging percentage above .450 (.457) and a strikeout rate below 20% (14.7%). The other three: Yordan Alvarez (.601 SLG%, 17.3% K-rate), Junior Caminero (.524 SLG%, 18.4% K-rate) and Miguel Vargas (.474 SLG%, 17.9% K-rate).

While it did not officially count toward his case, it's worth noting that DeLauter seemed to level up in October, hitting .310/.396/.452 with more walks (6) than strikeouts (4) across Cleveland's 11 postseason contests. Even as the Guardians' offense sputtered, DeLauter delivered quality at-bats and was a menace for both Chicago's and Tampa Bay's pitching staffs.

Tolle was terrific, too. Watching him emerge as one of Boston's best pitchers and one of the league's most likable personalities was a highlight of the 2026 season. Having begun the season in Triple-A, Tolle's late start prevented him from accumulating a major-league workload on par with Messick's, but he was similarly excellent on a per-inning basis.

I could have gone in a number of directions with my final spot. There was another Guardians standout in Travis Bazzana, who was named an All-Star as a rookie but faded badly in August before finishing strong in September. The White Sox had a pair of rock-solid rookie contributors in outfielders Tristan Peters and Sam Antonacci. Even the last-place Royals had Carter Jensen, an impressively reliable power source (27 HR, .467 SLG%) and an exciting next chapter behind the plate as Kansas City prepares for life after Salvador Perez.

There was also Toronto's Kazuma Okamoto, a bright spot in an otherwise dismal season for the Blue Jays' offense, and Rule 5 pick Spencer Miles, one of the best multi-inning relievers in the American League. Athletics outfielder Henry Bolte ranked 10th among position players in fWAR from Aug. 1 through the end of the season. I even took a look at hard-throwing Angels right-hander Walbert Urena, whose surface-level numbers (2.97 ERA in 148 ⅓ innings) were eye-catching but whose peripherals didn't quite measure up.

Ultimately, though, I thought Murakami's memorable rookie campaign warranted inclusion on my ballot. Chicago's spectacular and speedy turnaround from deep rebuild to a postseason appearance was one of the biggest stories of the 2026 season, and Murakami was too big a part of that tale to ignore. I wanted his introduction to the major leagues — as much of a roller coaster ride as it was from start to finish — represented on my ballot, so he earned my fifth and final vote.

Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

#2684. A cleared Deshaun Watson, a rising Shedeur Sanders and a Browns QB decision on hold

CLEVELAND (AP) — Even though Deshaun Watson has been cleared from the concussion protocol, it isn't certain he'll be the Cleveland Browns' starting quarterback for this week's game against his former team, the Houston Texans.

Coach Todd Monken said on Monday that he wasn't ready to name a quarterback since he still wants to evaluate Sunday's 23-22 overtime loss to the New Orleans Saints with the offensive coaching staff.

Shedeur Sanders was solid in his first start of the season, completing 19 of 31 passes for 297 yards and two touchdowns.

"It's week to week. A player doesn't lose or win a job ... I don't know what that means. Each week we put the best players on the field that give us a chance to win," said Monken when he was asked if he believes a player can lose their starting job due to injury.

Monken also didn't set a timeline for when he would tap either Watson or Sanders as this week's starter. Sanders' late-game performance showed Monken that the second-year quarterback and son of Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders is showing signs of development.

"There were moments at the end of the game where he made plays," Monken said. "He got it in the players' hands and did a really good job. He was in command. So, I was really pleased for him and I was hopeful he played well. I thought he had a great week of practice, and there is no guarantee that that will carry over.

"It gives me more and more confidence in what I saw in the fall, that there's something to build on, for sure."

Monken decided to go for the win after Harold Fannin Jr.'s 39-yard touchdown in overtime, but Sanders was pressured on the 2-point conversion and couldn't complete his pass to Denzel Boston after rolling right. Even if Boston would have caught it, the play would have been nullified because right tackle Tytus Howard was called for holding.

Monken said Sanders didn't have a chance to complete a quick throw.

"They did a good job with their corners of disrupting us at the line of scrimmage," Monken said. "We didn't get to the spots we needed to get to, so could've even sat in there a little bit, of course, but we got disrupted and that threw us off a little bit."

After only three home games in the first nine weeks, the Browns are home for five weeks, including their bye week, and don't hit the road again until Dec. 19 against the New York Giants. Even though there is some disappointment at being 5-4 after consecutive losses for the first time this season, Monken tried to stress the positives to his players after the close loss in New Orleans.

"We've earned being 5-4," he said. "We're right there in the mix. I do believe our best football is ahead of us, and I wanted our guys to know that we made it through a pretty damn hard grind of having six of your first nine on the road. We're 3-0 at home. Guess what? We have the next four at home and a bye week.

"It's all right there in front of us. It really is."

Sanders was 3 of 5 for 154 yards and a touchdown on downfield attempts (throws of 10 air yards or more). All five attempts happened after halftime.

The Browns have allowed opponents to score on the opening possession in all but one game this season. The 41 points allowed on first drives are tied with Miami for the worst in the league. Five of those drives ended in touchdowns, while the Saints were the third team to score on a field goal.

Boston and KC Concepcion became the first rookie wide receiver duo to both have at least 85 yards receiving in the same game since Amari Cooper and Seth Roberts did it for the Oakland Raiders in 2015. Boston had six catches for 98 yards and Concepcion added four receptions for 85 yards and his first touchdown.

Safety Grant Delpit had a rough day in his hometown, allowing five receptions for 41 yards. He got caught flat-footed on Juwan Johnson's 15-yard touchdown in overtime.

The Browns left New Orleans without any significant injuries.

7 — Consecutive field goals made by Andre Szmyt of 50 yards or more.

Cleveland will host Houston on Sunday. Watson made his Browns debut against the Texans in 2022, completing 12 of 22 passes for 131 yards in a 27-14 victory.

#2683. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2680. 2026 MLB Gold Glove winners: Pete Crow-Armstrong wins second honor, Red Sox and D-backs lead with three each

The winners of the 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove were announced Sunday night by Major League Baseball and, as expected, Cubs wunderkind Pete Crow-Armstrong took home his second straight National League Gold Glove in center field. PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. #2679. Jonathan Taylor Trade Rumors: Vikings, Broncos, Packers among potential landing spots as deadline approaches

Jonathan Taylor is the talk of the town after the Colts shifted their stance on trading him. I'll be cataloging every trade rumor and update we get on the situation in this article, starting with a big update.

11/7 Update: The Ringer's Tom Pelissero believes Taylor is staying in Indy. The Colts are looking for a blockbuster haul and no team has made them an offer. This is by no means the end of the saga, but it's increasingly likely that the Colts' unreasonable ask for Taylor prices out all interested parties.

The Vikings make too much sense. They have possibly the best defense in the NFL and a weak passing attack. Given that a superstar quarterback isn't walking through the door anytime soon, they should be an old-school, ground-and-pound offense that complements the defense for low-scoring wins. They don't have the horses for that in their backfield right now. Aaron Jones has had a solid season while averaging 4.2 yards per carry, but he can't make it through a game without picking up a new injury. Jordan Mason, on the other hand, has missed time with an injury of his own and is plodding his way to 3.9 yards per attempt. Minnesota also has extra draft capital in 2027 via the Jonathan Greenard trade, which netted them the Eagles' third-round pick.

The Broncos were reportedly the team that nearly outbid the Texans for David Montgomery in the offseason. Jonah Coleman has emerged as a solid option for them, but RJ Harvey is on injured reserve and J.K. Dobbins—now relegated to backup duties—is averaging a dreary 3.3 yards per carry. Taylor would immediately take over as the workhorse back on a team that has failed to create a successful ground game for Sean Payton's entire tenure as head coach. Local reporter Zac Stevens makes it sound like they are pushing hard to get a deal done.

11/8 Update: NFL insider Josina Anderson says that the Giants have pulled out of conversations to acquire Taylor. Things change quickly in the NFL, but this sounds fairly definitive.

11/9 Update: While the Giants are reportedly out of the Taylor trade talks, their offer has been revealed. They were reportedly willing to part ways with second- and fifth-round picks for Taylor. The Colts declined, though that was likely to continue fielding offers. This might be the best deal they get. It would not be surprising for the Colts to circle back on this offer ahead of tomorrow's deadline.

Cam Skattebo's weird season makes the Taylor trade even more viable. He leads all running backs in fumbles and was benched after losing the ball in overtime versus the Commanders. Skattebo came back with a vengeance in Week 7 with a 17/124/1 rushing line, but he also went down with a hamstring injury at the end of the game. It held him out of Week 9's contest, though it looks like he will be back for Week 10. With his minor injury and Tyrone Tracy on IR, the Giants could view running back as a need regardless of the availability of Taylor. The fact that a superstar happens to be up for grabs is simply fortuitous timing.

The Packers are the last of the big four teams routinely linked to Taylor, including by NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, who didn't list the Seahawks or Bengals. Though that's simply pulling from the ticker on his Sunday morning segment.

11/9 Update: The Packers were already getting nothing out of their ground game, and now Jacobs is hurt. He has a fractured finger, though there's a chance he manages to play through it in Week 10. Still, Jacobs has been dreadfully inefficient this year and has ongoing legal troubles.

The injury could be the nudge Green Bay needed to pull the trigger on Taylor.

Schefter didn't specifically mention the Bengals in his Sunday morning hit, but NFL insider Jordan Schultz has included them as a team to watch.

Cincy's rushing attack is struggling this year. They are 22nd in EPA per rush attempt and Chase Brown ranks 38th in yards after contact per carry. Samaje Perine is shockingly ahead of him in that metric, though he only ranks 30th. The Bengals' defense has improved this year, but it's not going to carry them to a title. Their path to hoisting the Lombardi Trophy ultimately runs through having the league's best offense. Taylor would round out an offense that already has an unstoppable passing attack.

This destination continues to look less likely by the week. Schultz included Seattle in his list of teams interested in Taylor, but he's in the minority of reporters in that regard. The Seahawks just got first-round pick Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet back from stints on IR. Seattle trusts Charbonnet to do the dirty work and doesn't have much tape on Price because of the month he spent on injured reserve. It would be surprising for them to throw in the towel on Price after just four games.

At 4-4, they might not feel confident in pushing their chips in for the 2026 season either. The Giants at -160 (61.5 percent) are considerably more likely to make the playoffs than Seattle at -138 (58 percent), if you take DraftKings' numbers at face value. Seattle is undoubtedly a better offense when they have an elite running back to lean on. Given Sam Darnold's middling play this year, they are likely a team that benefits more than the average roster from a great running back. But their investment in Price and shaky start make a trade unlikely.

The Commanders stick out as a logical fit for Taylor, but reporters aren't bringing them up at all, so I'll keep this brief. Even at 2-4-1, they're still in the hunt for the NFC East crown. Their Week 10 game versus the Giants will have a massive impact on their place in the standings. With Jacory Croskey-Merritt on IR, Kaytron Allen waived, Jeremy McNichols potentially done for the year with a foot injury, and Jerome Ford waived, almost every notable member of the backfield is out of the picture. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler are the last ones standing. For a team with a dynamic, dual-threat quarterback, the Commanders do not have a running back who can take advantage of the extra attention defenses pay to Jayden Daniels. The Commanders will likely do their due diligence regarding Taylor, but the lack of buzz connecting them to the trade talks likely means they're not in the running.

It's worth mentioning that the Colts aren't obligated to trade Taylor. Their asking price of a CMC-level haul could price all potential partners out.

Taylor is an elite runner, but McCaffrey's abilities as a receiver haven't been matched by anyone since Marshall Faulk. McCaffrey was also 26 when he was traded. Taylor is 27 and will turn 28 at the end of the regular season. There are enough interested parties and a desire to make this happen from the Colts' end that I bet a deal gets done, but it's not a foregone conclusion.

#2677. MLB Power Rankings: Brewers end 2026 season at No. 1 as World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

It's a juggernaut of an organization. They churn out talent and get the most out of every player they have. They seem to trade away talent at the exact right time. They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

The Brewers head to next season with plenty of question marks, but they'll answer them. They always do. They are the champions of Major League Baseball and they sit atop the final 2026 Power Rankings.

Looking forward to next spring, my expectation is the Brewers will be No. 1. Some years, I write about why the defending champion is not No. 1. I've long since learned my lesson with this team, though. No more. The Brewers will be No. 1 heading into spring training.

#2669. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.

#2668. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2665. Game Recap: Saints host Browns in Week 9 clash

The New Orleans Saints were back in action after the bye week when the Cleveland Browns visited the Big Easy on Sunday afternoon. Here's a full recap of the matchup.

Cleveland began the game by going three-and-out, before Audric Estime got the Saints offense going straight away with three runs totalling 32 yards.

Tyler Shough then found Juwan Johnson for 19 more with his first throw, but a few unsuccessful runs and a sack later, the Saints were held to a field goal attempt.

Charlie Smyth converted from 30 yards to give the black and gold an early lead.

The Browns were then forced into another quick punt as the Saints defense got off to a strong start.

Shough found Chris Olave for 11 yards before breaking off for a 14-yard run, but it was soon another field goal attempt after he was sacked on 3rd down.

This time, Smyth was no good from 52 yards, and the score remained 3-0.

Shadeur Sanders found the first big play of the game for Cleveland with a 16-yard pass to Dylan Sampson, who also had a few short gains on the ground as the Browns drove past midfield.

After being stuffed short of the chains on 3rd down, a 41-yard field goal from Andre Szmyt tied the game.

Shough then copied a play from Paris with a 52-yard bomb downfield to Barion Brown as the Saints sought to regain the lead.

But a play later, Jordyn Tyson fumbled after making a catch, which the defense fell on to return possession to the Browns.

New Orleans was able to force another quick punt out of the Browns, but Brown fumbled on the return. Cleveland fell on it in the red zone.

A penalty against Carl Granderson helped the visitors set up 1st-and-goal, but he made up for it by sacking Sanders to push them back.

A few plays later, Sanders was just short of the goal line on 3rd-and-goal. The Browns offense stayed out there, and the Saints were able to come out big with a stop on 4th down to keep the game at 3-3.

Shough connected with Olave for 36 yards to move the Saints out from deep in their own territory, but after another pass for just one yard and two incompletions, they were forced to punt just before the half.

New Orleans went three-and-out and punted to begin the second half, before Sanders scrambled for 11 yards on 3rd down to avoid the same fate.

He then completed a 60-yard pass to Denzel Boston to set up 1st-and-goal.

But the Saints' defense came up huge once again, with a tackle-for-loss, sack, and incompletion from Sanders limiting Cleveland to a chip-shot field goal that gave them a 6-3 lead.

Shough responded with a scoring drive of his own, on a 54-yard drive highlighted by a 12-yard pass to Noah Fant and his own scrambles moving the ball down the field.

Smyth's 27-yard kick tied the game at 6-6.

Cleveland then went three-and-out as Granderson got to the quarterback once again, but New Orleans would do the same, which gave the visitors the ball to begin the fourth.

Sanders got the ball to midfield with a 10-yard pass to KC Concepcion, but failed to find another first down. He threw an incomplete pass to Sampson on 4th-and-2, and the Saints took over on downs again.

Taking advantage of the shorter field, Shough moved the black and gold into field goal range with a 9-yard throw to Tyson.

After being sacked by Myles Harden, the Saints were forced into yet another field goal, which Smyth converted from 48 yards.

But the lead didn't last long, as Sanders threw a 64-yard touchdown to Concepcion on the opening play of the ensuing drive to give Cleveland a 13-9 advantage.

New Orleans then went three-and-out, before Cleveland had another punt of their own around the two-minute warning.

Needing a touchdown, Shough found Olave for 33 yards to move the drive into the red zone. He then found Alvin Kamara for 8 more, before Estime ran in the 2-yard score to re-establish the lead for the black and gold.

But Sanders threw twice for a total of 37 yards to Jerry Jeudy, which set up a field goal that Szmyt converted from 51 yards to force overtime.

The Saints received first, and Kamara broke off three big runs as the ball moved past midfield.

Shough then found Devaughn Vele for 9 yards before Estime ran for 9 more.

Shough ran for 8 yards before finding Vele again, setting up a 15-yard touchdown throw to Johnson to give the black and gold a 23-16 lead.

Needing a touchdown of their own, two passes from Sanders to Boston helped Cleveland into Saints territory.

Sanders then found Harold Fannin Jr for a 39-yard touchdown.

Cleveland opted to go for two and the win, which is where the Saints came up with the biggest stop of the day as Sanders' pass intended for Boston fell incomplete.

New Orleans held on 23-22 to set up a huge divisional matchup next weekend with the Carolina Panthers.
